Week 01 — Getting Started with R

From wide to long, grouping and summarizing, measures of central tendency and variability, and a first pass at ggplot2

Authors

Johann-Friedrich Salzmann

Joshua Elias Schmidt Rodrigues

Date

September 9, 2026

Package management

Same as every session: bootstrap pacman, then load the tidyverse.

if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")
Loading required package: pacman

p_load(tidyverse)

Where we left off

R/RStudio/Git, objects, data structures (vectors, matrices, data frames, arrays, lists), indexing/subsetting, and loading data are all Intro R course material — see the Intro R course repository (Day 1 for objects/data structures/indexing, Day 3 for loading data formats). We pick up straight from real, already-familiar data.

Warm-up: from wide to long

The same Bundestag polling data from the Intro R course, still wide (one column per party) — originally sourced from ZEIT ONLINE’s polling tracker.

polls <- read_csv("data/polls.csv")

Warm-up: grouping and summarizing

Grouping by two variables at once, same idea as the toy cat1/cat2 tibble from Intro R Day 3 — one row per party x year here.

polls_long |>
  mutate(year = year(Date)) |>
  group_by(party, year) |>
  summarize(avg_share = mean(share, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(party, year)
`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by party and year.
ℹ Output is grouped by party.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(party, year))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.

Collapsing to one row per party only.

party_avg <- polls_long |>
  group_by(party) |>
  summarize(avg_share = mean(share, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_share))
party_avg

Warm-up: plotting the result

Real party colors, same vector as Intro R Day 2/3.

party_colors <- c(
  CDUCSU = "#000000",
  SPD    = "#E3000F",
  Gruene = "#46962b",
  FDP    = "#ffed00",
  Linke  = "#be3075",
  AfD    = "#009ee0",
  BSW    = "#7d3f98"
)

A bar chart of the summarize() result.

party_avg |>
  ggplot(aes(x = party, y = avg_share, fill = party)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = party_colors) +
  labs(title = "Average Bundestag polling share, 2017-today", x = NULL, y = "Share (%)")

And the full trend line — exactly Intro R Day 2/3’s central plot.

polls_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = share, color = party)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = party_colors) +
  labs(title = "Bundestag polling trend", x = NULL, y = "Share (%)", color = "Party")
`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'

Warning: Removed 1548 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_smooth()`).

Measures of central tendency: the mean

x <- 1:5
x
[1] 1 2 3 4 5
mean(x)
[1] 3
sum(x) / length(x)
[1] 3

This only makes sense for numeric vectors.

x_char <- c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e")
mean(x_char)
Warning in mean.default(x_char): argument is not numeric or logical: returning
NA

[1] NA

But it does work for logicals — TRUE counts as 1, FALSE as 0.

x_logical <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
mean(x_logical)
[1] 0.6
sum(x_logical)
[1] 3

The same mean again, now via a tibble and summarize() — from here on we keep working with tibbles for every aggregation.

x_tbl <- tibble(xcol = x)
x_tbl |> summarize(mean_x = mean(xcol))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_x
   <dbl>
1      3

Central tendency and variability, the rest of the toolbox

Mean: mean(). Median: median(). Variance: var(). Standard deviation: sd(). Range: range(). Inter-quartile range: IQR(). Pooling every party’s share into one number is illustrative only — a real analysis would do this per party, as in the Try it below.

polls_long |>
  summarize(
    mean_share   = mean(share, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_share = median(share, na.rm = TRUE),
    var_share    = var(share, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_share     = sd(share, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_share    = min(share, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_share    = max(share, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr_share    = IQR(share, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  mean_share median_share var_share sd_share min_share max_share iqr_share
       <dbl>        <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1       14.9           13      73.2     8.56         2        40      12.5

The mode: three definitions

R has no dedicated mode() function. One small tibble to work with — shares (numeric): 3 and 7 tied at 3 occurrences each, everyone else a singleton. parties (character), same length: SPD is the single clear winner, no tie.

mode_data <- tibble(
  shares  = c(3, 7, 3, 9, 7, 2, 3, 7, 5, 1),
  parties = c("SPD", "CDUCSU", "SPD", "Gruene", "SPD", "AfD", "SPD", "Linke", "FDP", "CDUCSU")
)
mode_data
# A tibble: 10 × 2
   shares parties
    <dbl> <chr>  
 1      3 SPD    
 2      7 CDUCSU 
 3      3 SPD    
 4      9 Gruene 
 5      7 SPD    
 6      2 AfD    
 7      3 SPD    
 8      7 Linke  
 9      5 FDP    
10      1 CDUCSU

select() the column we need, then group_by() + summarize(n()) — the way we already know.

shares_counts <- mode_data |>
  select(shares) |>
  group_by(shares) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  ungroup()
shares_counts
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  shares     n
   <dbl> <int>
1      1     1
2      2     1
3      3     3
4      5     1
5      7     3
6      9     1

count() is a shortcut for that same group_by()+summarize(n())+ungroup() combination, in one step — used here for parties.

parties_counts <- mode_data |>
  select(parties) |>
  count(parties)
parties_counts
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  parties     n
  <chr>   <int>
1 AfD         1
2 CDUCSU      2
3 FDP         1
4 Gruene      1
5 Linke       1
6 SPD         4

Definition 1: every value tied for the highest count (multimodal).

shares_counts |>
  filter(n == max(n))
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  shares     n
   <dbl> <int>
1      3     3
2      7     3

Definition 2: a single “the” mode. filter()-ing for the max count alone isn’t safe here — we can’t know in advance whether there’s a tie, and if there were, every tied row would come back. arrange() + slice(1) always returns exactly one row, tie or not.

parties_counts |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  slice(1)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  parties     n
  <chr>   <int>
1 SPD         4

Definition 3: for numeric data, average the tied values into one number.

shares_counts |>
  filter(n == max(n)) |>
  summarize(mean_mode = mean(shares))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_mode
      <dbl>
1         5

Plotting data, revisited in ggplot2

Same ideas as Intro R Day 2, quickly, plus one new geom — the bivariate scatter is skipped here, since the warm-up trend line above already showed share over time.

polls_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of polled party shares", x = "Share (%)")
Warning: Removed 1548 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_bin()`).

polls_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share)) +
  geom_density() +
  labs(title = "Density of polled party shares", x = "Share (%)")
Warning: Removed 1548 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_density()`).

polls_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = share)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of polled party shares", x = NULL, y = "Share (%)")
Warning: Removed 1548 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).

A violin plot shows the full shape of the distribution, not just its quartiles.

polls_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = share)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(title = "Violin plot of polled party shares", x = NULL, y = "Share (%)")
Warning: Removed 1548 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_ydensity()`).

Try it: AfD’s historic high and low

Your task: populist parties’ support can swing dramatically over time — looking at AfD’s entire historic polling record (not just recent numbers), what’s the highest and lowest share it has ever been polled at?

afd <- polls_long |>
  filter(party == "AfD") |>
  arrange(desc(share))
afd |> slice(1)          # highest

Your task: different pollsters can paint quite different pictures — repeat this, but separately for each pollster: find AfD’s highest and lowest recorded share (and the date) per pollster.

# slice() is group-aware once grouped — same "verbs act per group" idea
# as Day 3, just applied to slice() this time. Shares are whole numbers,
# so ties are common: a trailing slice(1) always narrows a tie down to
# one representative row per pollster
afd |>                              # highest per pollster
  group_by(Pollster) |>
  arrange(desc(share)) |>
  slice(1)

Try it: how much did the polls agree right before the 2025 election?

Your task: the 2025 federal election was held 2025-02-23. Calculate the mean, variance, and standard deviation of the Green party’s polled share in the four weeks leading up to it, then plot the distribution of those final polls against the Greens’ actual result (11.6%).

gruene_pre_election <- polls_long |>
  filter(party == "Gruene", between(Date, as.Date("2025-01-26"), as.Date("2025-02-23")))
gruene_pre_election

 2 BT02250128N Forsa                   2025-01-28  2504 21.01.–27.0… Grue…  14  
 3 BT13250129C YouGov                  2025-01-29  1781 24.01.–27.0… Grue…  13  
 4 BT06250130F Forschungsgruppe Wahlen 2025-01-30  1428 27.01.–29.0… Grue…  14  
 5 BT01250130Q Infratest dimap         2025-01-30  1336 27.01.–29.0… Grue…  15

gruene_pre_election |>

  ggplot(aes(x = share)) +

  geom_vline(xintercept = 11.6, linetype = "dashed") +

Try it: BSW’s rise above — and fall back below — the 5% threshold

Your task: BSW is a newly founded party — founded 2024-01-08 — that had to clear the 5% electoral threshold to enter parliament at all. Look at the remainder of that year (2024-01-08 to 2024-12-31): mutate() a cleared_threshold column. Compute the average share per pollster for each above and below the threshold. Plot the distribution of BSW’s share by pollster.

bsw_2024 <- polls_long |>
  filter(party == "BSW", between(Date, as.Date("2024-01-08"), as.Date("2024-12-31")), !is.na(share)) |>
  mutate(cleared_threshold = if_else(share >= 5, "above 5%", "below 5%"))
